titleFa: کتاب Vision 3: English for Grade 12 (Student & Workbook)
author: Ministry of Education
introFa: کتاب «Vision 3: English for Grade 12 (Student & Workbook)» نوشته Ministry of Education یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح All Levels است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Vision 3: English for Grade 12 (Student & Workbook)»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: ‘Audiomobile’ is given to the first four tracks, and points at a compositional approach and a mode of listening which is continued in the final tracks. The notes reveal that the penulti- mate track is Gerhard’s first autonomous com- position, sadly consigned to the studio shelf after only one concert presentation while the final, and longest, track, Lament for the Death of a Bullfighter, is a dramatisation of a poem by Federico García Lorca. As well as adding a clear dramaturgy to the primarily gestural music that has preceded, the link with the poem also narrativises some of the sound. However, the clever curation means that, for the listener, by this point the abstract contexts of the sounds have already been established. The music seems also to contribute to a more absurd perception of the poem than might have been the case were this track the first on the disc. One has the impression that, in addition to considerable technical skill, Gerhard really has something to say musically. The André Stordeur discs come with less infor- mation than the Gerhard CD but a larger and more comprehensive set of pieces. The liner notes contain a good biography in English and French, along with programme notes for each piece written by the composer, each of which gives short details of the equipment and program- ming languages used, including early work in BASIC. These discs represent a contrasting approach to that of Gerhard: here, the music is presented in chronological order, there is an attempt at completeness in terms of the presenta- tion of the electronic work, and the musical mater- ial is drawn more from synthesizers than samples. Of the pieces on the first disc, entitled ‘18 Days 1978–1979’, Stordeur writes that he wants to offer an alternative to ‘cosmic electronic music’; one presumes that Stockhausen is the composer whose music he does not wish to evoke. This music is less gestural than that of Gerhard, and somewhat more linear. The most recent set of pieces on the third disc, ‘6 Synthesis Studies circa 2000’, have something of the 1960s about them. Stordeur writes that his studies with Chatur Lal and Ravi Shankar inspired him to create the sounds of Indian instruments and music with synthesizers, and his re-creation of these sounds is largely success- ful, resulting in music rich in harmonics and micro-details. However, these tracks feel more like technical demonstrations than musical experiments and it is unclear what the electronic rendering of these instruments offers that the ori- ginal instruments did not. The final study, Like Phil, not only evokes the sound of Einstein on the Beach but arguably mimics it, given the Glass ensemble’s reliance on synthesizers; out- side of the operatic context of Einstein this music sounds more like an exercise than a fin- ished piece. The second disc, ‘Analog and Digital Works, 1980–2000’ contains the most musically rewarding of all of the pieces in the collection. Oh Well, the most substantial of Stordeur’s works, makes space for more varied sounds and sound-sources, a more interesting and complex form, and a more harmonically complex approach. Chant 10a intro- duces a vocal sample, although not in the ‘cosmic’ sense that might be expected by the work’s title. In contrast to those on the other discs, these pieces feel musically autonomous: they are rich in filters, sweeps and psychoacoustic effects such as the Shepard tone, but also offer more in terms of musical narrative and differentiated lis- tening. As with Gerhard, the other works perhaps set up the context in which these can be heard but, in contrast, it is only in these pieces that the attention of the listener might really be held. There is a stylistic unity across Stordeur’s work from 1978–2000, but this perhaps makes the later works seem less impressive since musical development is not demonstrated in line with the technical development that took place during this period. His music evokes both Stockhausen and more popular electronica, despite his noted aversion to the ‘cosmic’. Both of these releases offer carefully curated, well-produced and nuanced pictures of the music of Roberto Gerhard and André Stordeur. The differences in instrumentality and approach may well cater for differing preferences but, in terms of the music and the quality of the infor- mation provided in the liner notes, the disc of Gerhard’s works is the standout of the two. Lauren Redhead ‘A TRIPLE PORTRAIT’: CHAMBER MUSIC BY ELENA FIRSOVA. Homage to Canisy2,3; Lost Vision3; A Triple Portrait1,2,3; Night Songs5,3; Spring Sonata1,3; For Slava2; Meditation in the Japanese Garden1,2,3; Three Poems of Osip Mandelstam4,3; Tender is the Sorrow1,2,3,6,7. Marsyas Trio (1Helen Vidovich (fl.), 2Valerie Wellbanks (vc), 3Fei Ren (pno)), 4Maacha Deubner (sop.), 5Hannah Pedley (mz), 6Patrick Dawkins (vln), 7Morgan Gough (vla). Meridian CDE 84635 Given the impact of Elena Firsova’s early years in the Soviet Union, it is perhaps not surprising that the poetry of Osip Mandelstam – a victim of Stalinist oppression in 1938 – should resonate cdS and dvdS 103

so deeply with her, but it is still striking how effectively she has responded to the verse’s eco- nomical expressiveness in the two sets of songs recorded here. Three Poems was written and per- formed in Russia a decade or so before Firsova finally moved to the West in 1991, while Night Songs (2009) is much more recent. With its rela- tively sparse accompaniments for flute and cello, this is a particularly intense and haunting com- position, the texts epitomising Mandelstam’s spe- cial ability to blend the mundane and the mysterious whilst Firsova’s music resists any temptation to indulge in nostalgic expansiveness, especially in the last of the three settings, which uses the names of her birth city, Leningrad/St Petersburg, with a telling mixture of joy and apprehensiveness. One can see why Firsova should once have commented how she learnt from Mandelstam ‘that we can speak very quiet- ly about the most important things, and that we can see the most tragic occurrences in the light of beauty’. The impact of Firsova’s Mandelstam settings is all the greater here for the contributions of two excellent singers – soprano Maacha Deubner in Three Poems, and mezzo soprano Hannah Pedley in Night Songs. What these vocal compositions can’t quite manage to do, however, is to turn the sequence of perfor- mances on the disc as a whole into a completely satisfying programme suited to continuous lis- tening. Fewer, larger-scale pieces of more diverse character might have achieved that, but the decision to base the collection around items that fit the forces of the Marsyas Trio (with additional violin and viola in the last work) results in a rather restricted expressive and textural palette. Five of the seven purely instrumental works date from the years 2007–12, and it is useful to hear how the Spring Sonata (1982) and Meditation in the Japanese Garden (1991) set the stylistic stage for so much of what follows. Spring Sonata, for flute and piano, is the earliest single-movement instrumental work included. Here, the 22-year-old composer reveals her familiarity with (I imagine) the likes of Denisov in ways guaranteed to annoy the Khrennikov- era musical establishment. Yet the predominance of decorative elaboration serves to prevent the more turbulent spirit evident at the piece’s cli- max from assuming dangerously Boulezian pro- portions. Meditation – originally scored for flute, viola and piano, but heard here in Firsova’s 2011 version for the Marsyas Trio – is perhaps overly true to its title, and although Firsova is too scrupulous an artist merely to ramble self-indulgently it is the music’s more explosive central section that lingers longest in the memory. The fact, though, that the Japanese garden in question was at Dartington, rather than somewhere further east, probably helped to inject a useful dose of reality and ensure that the piece avoids the clichés of a pseudo-Oriental fantasy. Russian associations also inflect two of the more successful recent pieces, both elegiac. For Slava (2007) avoids the kind of sentimental pathos that any heartfelt homage to the great cellist could so easy slide into, with the eerie har- monics of its final stages bringing a bracingly stark austerity and sense of loss to the scene. Similarly, Tender is the sorrow, written in 2010 as an ‘In Memoriam’ for a cherished family member, manages not to overindulge in nostal- gia for an irrecoverable past: here too something of that salutary Mandelstamian economy emerges, with what the poet describes as ‘a quiet argument . . . between the approaching twilight and the fading ray of light’. It is Baudelaire rather than Mandelstam whom Firsova evokes with her most direct trib- ute to the admirable Marsyas Trio, A Triple Portrait (2011). At a little more than 11 minutes in total, this is the most substantial of the disc’s instrumental works, and it provides a good syn- opsis of the composer’s preoccupations with pas- sing time and fading yet still potent memories. Just occasionally, when she allows herself to rage ‘against the dying of the light’, we glimpse deeper and darker dimensions, and it is with these that possible debts to Shostakovich, Prokofiev and even earlier Russian masters might be sensed. At a time when modernism, in the manner of Birtwistle or Boulez, is slowly fading away as a model of choice for younger composers, Firsova’s music makes a plausible case for such deeper, darker echoes.
